bridge: Builds on W06 path boundaries and B03 schemas. Use the supplied metadata cases; no executable upload is required.
teaching:
Uploading has several boundaries: accepting bytes, deciding type/size, storing an object and later serving it. A filename or client Content-Type is a claim, not a proof of content. Validation should reflect what the application genuinely supports and should use maintained parsers where parsing is needed.

Store uploads under server-controlled names outside executable application paths. Keep ownership metadata and serve content through a deliberate policy, including response type and disposition. Prevent overwriting existing objects by guessed names. Do not expose processing tools to unlimited size or decompression work.

A secure design specifies what happens at each failure stage. A file accepted for storage may still be quarantined pending processing, and a parser failure should not fall back to serving untrusted active content. Separate access control from content validation: a valid image belonging to B must not become readable by A.

To understand the lab’s tiny PHP example, echo writes a value into the response and file_get_contents reads a resource supported by that PHP environment. The demonstrated upload is executed because of that server’s file-handler configuration, not because the filename has magical powers. You only need to trace this boundary; this lesson’s metadata exercise does not ask you to create or run a web shell.
example:
Practice policy: text-only notes, max 100 UTF-8 bytes
Store under generated IDs; never execute or interpret as HTML.
Cases:
1. owner A, 20 bytes UTF-8 text -> accept private object
2. owner A, 101 bytes text -> reject size
3. owner A, claimed text but invalid UTF-8 -> reject decode
4. filename ../one.txt -> ignore as storage path; generated ID
5. owner B object requested by A -> deny read
explanation: This intentionally narrow policy is fully testable without guessing complex file types. The original filename can be retained as safely displayed metadata, but never becomes an executable/storage path. A generated identifier still needs collision-safe creation and ownership checking.
exercise: Build a decision table for the five supplied cases. Add an empty file case and state whether your policy permits it. Explain how you would return text containing demo without converting it into HTML.
solution: Case 1 accepts the private A-owned object; case 2 rejects 101 bytes; case 3 rejects invalid UTF-8; case 4 never uses ../one.txt as a storage path and can accept otherwise valid bytes under a generated ID; case 5 denies A access to B’s object. For this reference policy choose to reject empty files as a user-input error; permitting them could also be valid if documented consistently. Serve the marker as text/plain under the chosen safe download/display policy, never by inserting it as HTML. Count UTF-8 bytes, not just characters: some characters require multiple bytes.
challenge: Extend the design with a background processor that can fail. Define pending, accepted and rejected states and give one access-control check in each. Explain why processing failure must not accidentally publish the raw object.
challenge_solution: Example lifecycle: pending means uploaded but not yet approved; only the owner may see status, not download raw content. Accepted means validation/processing succeeded; download still checks the current owner. Rejected means processing failed or policy disallowed it; owner may see a safe reason but the raw object stays unavailable. A worker must check it is updating the intended owned object, and an error must not silently set accepted or publish the storage URL. Decide cleanup and retry rules explicitly.
